preamble: It is the last week of the summer term. Reuben and his friend Ilya have offered to help their teacher clear out the school's lost-property cupboard.
body:
Miss Bhatt asked for two volunteers and Reuben's hand went up before he had decided anything about it.

The lost-property cupboard was a room at the end of the corridor by the hall, with a sloping ceiling and a light you had to hold the switch down for. When he pulled the door back the smell came out ahead of the coats, chlorine and old banana, and Ilya said he was going to die in here and it would be on Miss Bhatt.

She gave them two boxes and a bin bag. Named things went in the first box to be returned. Everything with no name went in the second, which was going to the charity collection on Friday morning. The bin bag was for anything with the sole coming off it.

Ilya did it the way he did everything, at speed, holding each item up for half a second before deciding. Reuben turned the collars out and read them. Some of the names had gone the colour of weak tea and some had been done in the sort of laundry pen that outlasts the jumper, and he found a cardigan belonging to a girl who had left in Year Four and put it in the returns box anyway.

"When we're in Year Six," Ilya said, "we get the lockers by the science room. The tall ones. Not those little ones by the gym."

"These are all size nine," Reuben said. He had four grey jumpers across his arms, all of them size nine, none of them named.

"And you're in my group for Whitby. I've already told Miss. I said it before Kyle could ask."

Reuben held up a swimming hat that had perished into something like a dried leaf and asked whether that went in the bag or the box.

At half past two Miss Bhatt put her head round the door to see how far they had got, and Reuben asked her where the charity bags actually went afterwards. A warehouse, she said. Leeds, she thought, or somewhere near it, and then out to shops all over the place. He asked if that was far. She said far enough, and laughed, and he laughed as well, slightly after her.

Ilya found a Manchester United sock and became busy with it for a while.

The navy jumper was under a pair of trousers nobody was ever going to claim. The cuffs had gone thin and there was a mark on the front from a Sports Day two years ago. Reuben knew before he turned the collar out whose it was, because he knew the shape of the capitals his mum used and he knew she pressed too hard with the pen. He held it a moment. Then he put it in the Friday box, low down, underneath the swimming things, and pushed it flat with the heel of his hand so it lay level with the rest. Then he took the folded paper out of his blazer pocket, looked at the edge of it and put it back without opening it.

On the way to fetch the second bin bag he passed the noticeboard. The sheet for September football trials had eleven names on it in eleven different pens. There was plenty of room left at the bottom.

"You've missed a cupboard," Ilya said, when he came back. "There's another one. In the annexe. Miss said we can do that one on Monday and get out of spellings."

"Monday's fine," Reuben said.

At half three Miss Bhatt came in properly to check what they had put where, and lifted the top layer out of the Friday box. She got to the navy jumper and turned it over and found the collar.

"Reuben. This one's got your name in it."

"It's all right," he said. "It won't fit me next year."

She looked at him for a second or two longer than the answer needed. Then she folded it the way he had folded it, low down, underneath, and pressed the flaps of the box shut.
